title: Model Dependence of Socioeconomic Associations with ADL Deterioration After Hospitalisation: Parallel Longitudinal Analyses of the Health and Retirement Study and CHARLS
content: Background. Hospitalisation in later life frequently occurs during a period of functional vulnerability. Socioeconomic differences in subsequent change in activities of daily living (ADL) may help identify groups that need closer follow-up, but reported associations can depend on which health and functional characteristics are adjusted for. We examined whether education and household wealth were associated with ADL deterioration and whether these associations were stable across successively adjusted models in two health-system contexts. Methods. We analysed the Health and Retirement Study (HRS; waves 13-15, 2016-2020) and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS; waves 2-4, 2013-2018) as two parallel cohorts. Eligible respondents were aged 50 years or older, reported hospitalisation between the baseline and follow-up waves, and had ADL measured at both waves. ADL deterioration was defined as a higher ADL difficulty count at follow-up than at baseline. A fixed nested sequence was used: age and sex plus education and wealth; addition of marital status, chronic conditions and depressive symptoms; and further addition of baseline ADL and IADL difficulty. Sensitivity analyses included respondent weighting, alternative outcome definitions, multiple imputation, expanded wealth imputation, death-inclusive models and E-values. Results. ADL deterioration occurred in 604 of 2,892 HRS respondents with an observed outcome (20.9%) and 454 of 1,691 CHARLS respondents with an observed outcome (26.8%). In HRS, the wealth OR moved from 0.788 (95% CI 0.718-0.866) in the socioeconomic model to 0.847 (0.765-0.938) after clinical adjustment and 0.857 (0.773-0.950) after further adjustment for baseline function. The education OR was 0.944 (0.916-0.973), 0.949 (0.920-0.979) and 0.947 (0.917-0.977), respectively. In CHARLS, the wealth OR was 0.827 (0.708-0.965; p = 0.016) before clinical adjustment, 0.855 (0.730-1.001; p = 0.051) after clinical adjustment and 0.853 (0.727-1.002; p = 0.053) after further adjustment for baseline function. Respondent-weighted multiple-imputation and community-cluster estimates in CHARLS remained compatible with no association (0.892, 95% CI 0.744-1.070; expanded wealth imputation 0.896, 0.777-1.034). CHARLS education estimates were too imprecise to support a gradient. Conclusions. Socioeconomic associations with ADL deterioration were not equivalently robust across cohorts. HRS showed an inverse wealth association across the nested models, whereas the CHARLS wealth signal weakened mainly with clinical adjustment and was not stable under missing-data and weighting scenarios. Most attenuation occurred at the clinical-covariate step, not after adding baseline function. These results argue for reporting model dependence and cohort heterogeneity explicitly; they do not establish a universal socioeconomic gradient, causality or clinical prediction.
